title: Reading Al-Fatiha

bigIdea.text: Al-Fatiha uses almost everything you have learned: harakat, sukun, shadda, long vowels, small alifs, the joining hamza and sun letters. Read it ayah by ayah, then all together.

proper.text: In this text Al-Fatiha has 7 ayat, and the basmala is ayah 1 (1:1).

What to look for: small alifs in 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:6 and 1:7; a joining hamza to glide past in every ayah except 1:5; sun letters after 'al-' in 1:1, 1:3, 1:4, 1:6 and 1:7; moon letters after 'al-' in 1:2, 1:6 and 1:7.

provenance.source: rebuilt cpfair/quran-tajweed annotations (madd_2, hamzat_wasl, lam_shamsiyyah) and Tanzil text for 1:1–1:7

proper.text: Stop and breathe at the end of each ayah. While you are learning, don't stop inside an ayah.

Every ayah of Al-Fatiha ends with a long vowel just before its last letter. When you stop there you may hold it 2, 4 or 6 counts: choose one length and keep it the same at every ayah end. The last word (1:7) has a maddah before a shadda: always 6 counts.

steps: Read it slowly, syllable by syllable
Read all seven ayat in a row

memoryHook.text: Seven ayat: stop and breathe at each end.

extras.text: Counting the basmala as the first ayah of Al-Fatiha is the Kufan way of numbering, which the Hafs mushaf follows.
Persian/Urdu readers: watch ح (1:1, 1:2, 1:3), ع (1:2, 1:5, 1:7) and ض (1:7). Don't flatten them into ه, ء or a 'z'.

note.text: Glide past the ٱ of the second, third and fourth words; the third and fourth have a sun letter (ر) after 'al-'.
You start on 'al-' before ح (a moon letter, lam said). The last word has a small alif.
Two sun lams before ر; a small alif in the first word.
A small alif on the first letter; a sun letter (د) after 'al-' in the last word.
Two doubled ي, each followed by a long alif; ع in the second and fourth words.
Start with 'i'; glide past the ٱ of the next two words (sun letter ص, then moon letter م).
The longest ayah (9 words). The last word has a maddah before a shadda: 6 counts.

drills.prompt: Read 1:1 to 1:7 by yourself once, slowly, stopping at each ayah end; then compare with Sheikh al-Minshawi.

questions.q: How many ayat does Al-Fatiha have in this text?
explain: Right: 1:1 to 1:7, with the basmala as 1:1.
6 would leave out the basmala, which is ayah 1 here.

questions.q: Where should a beginner stop in Al-Fatiha?
options: At the end of each ayah
In the middle of each ayah
Only at the end of the surah
explain: Stopping inside an ayah can break the meaning.
The ayat are short enough to stop at each end.

questions.q: In 1:1, how do you read the ٱ at the start of the second word?
options: Glide past it: join the first word straight to the lam
explain: A joining hamza is skipped when you read on.
There is no pause sign there.
ٱ is not a madd letter.

questions.q: The last word of Al-Fatiha has a maddah before a shadda. How long is it held?
explain: Too short for a maddah before a shadda.
4 is for other cases; here it is 6.
One count is a short vowel.

questions.q: At an ayah end, a long vowel comes just before the last letter. What is the rule for you when you stop there?
options: Choose 2, 4 or 6 counts and keep the same length at every ayah end
Never stop at the ayah end
explain: It is a long vowel, so at least 2.
Ayah ends are the right places to stop.

questions.q: How is the small alif on the first letter of 1:4 read?
explain: A small alif is a full long vowel.

questions.q: In 1:2 the first word starts with 'al-' before ح. Is the lam said?
options: Yes: ح is a moon letter, so the lam has sukun and is said
No: ح is a sun letter
explain: Only sun letters absorb the lam.

questions.q: In 1:4 the last word has 'al-' before د. What happens?
options: The lam is silent and د is doubled (a sun letter)
The lam is said with sukun
Both the lam and د are silent
explain: That would be a moon letter.

questions.q: You start 1:6. Its first word begins with ٱ. Which vowel do you start with?
options: No vowel: start on the second letter
explain: 'u' would need a damma on the third letter.
The second letter is sakin; you can't start on it.

questions.q: Why keep your ayah-end lengths the same through the surah?
options: Consistency is part of correct recitation
It is only needed in prayer
The mushaf marks each one differently
explain: These ends carry no special sign.

questions.q: What is the best way to learn to read Al-Fatiha?
options: Ayah by ayah: listen, read slowly, echo, then join
Read all seven at full speed from day one
Memorise the sounds without looking at the text
Read only the first and last ayat
explain: This lesson is about reading the text.

questions.q: In 1:5 the first word has a shadda on ي. How do you read it?
options: Close on ي after the 'i', then 'yaa'
explain: Right: the doubled ي splits across two syllables.
The shadda needs a closing ي and an opening one.

questions.q: In 1:7 the second word starts with ٱ and a lam with shadda. Reading on from the first word, what do you do?
options: Glide past ٱ straight into the doubled lam
Say 'al-' with a clear lam, then the doubled lam
explain: A joining hamza drops when you read on.
There is no pause sign there.
Only the doubled lam is heard.

remnote: Al-Fatiha in this mushaf (Hafs) == 7 ayat, with the basmala as 1:1
Where a beginner stops in Al-Fatiha == At the end of each ayah
Last word of Al-Fatiha (maddah before a shadda) == 6 counts
Long vowel before the last letter when you stop at an ayah end == 2, 4 or 6 counts: choose one and keep it
taskNow: Record yourself reading Al-Fatiha from 1:1 to 1:7, stopping and breathing at each ayah end, then self-rate it against Sheikh al-Minshawi.
